we propose a profile-dependent support vector machine for therapeutic drug monitoring, which incorporates a prior knowledge in the form of a priori information about the patient, such as age, gender, weight, and so on, and that we compare the performance of the proposed profile-dependent support vector machines with several neural network approaches.
the proposed approach is a useful tool for therapeutic drug monitoring in kidney recipients.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of support vector machines (SVNs) for the prediction of cyclosporine A blood levels in kidney transplant recipients.
the application of machine learning techniques to therapeutic drug monitoring of kidney transplant recipients, in which the prediction of CyA blood concentration is a key issue.
the application of a new approach based on SVMs and the use of prior knowledge for the prediction and detection of CyA blood concentrations in kidney transplant recipients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SVMs are the most suitable for the prediction of CyA blood concentrations, especially in the presence of noise.
the PD-SV approach is a good candidate for TDM of CyA in renal recipients.
the PD-SVMS approach is the best choice for the TDM of CyA in kidney recipients, and it can be used to individualize the dosage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a profile-dependent support vector machine is a promising approach for predicting CyA trough concentration in renal transplant recipients.
we have proposed a twofold SVM-based approach for TDM of kidney recipients, which includes the prediction and the detection tasks.
the proposed PD-SVMs are a useful, robust and understandable tool that could be used to aid the medical decision-making process for individualizing CyA dosage in renal transplant patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SVMs can be used as a robust tool for therapeutic drug monitoring.
the proposed PD-SVM approach can be used to improve the accuracy of TDM models, which in turn could lead to better patient outcomes.
the PD-SV approach is more robust than the standard SVM and the MLP, and it is more accurate than the MLP, in the presence of noise.
